# Volume 2 — XXI Sweet Miss Rosalind

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Classes commenced and Nell went back to her job, possessing a lot more experience though significantly fewer theories. Her new students numbered several, six- and seven-year-olds who were merely stepping, wide-eyed, into a marvel-filled world. Robin and Lucy were included in this group. Robin was seated alongside Milty Gammon, a pupil for a year already and thus rather a man of the world. At Sunday School on the preceding Sunday, Lucy had formed an agreement to sit beside Lily Mott; however, because Lily Mott failed to appear on day one, she was provisionally placed with Mirabel Cotton, a ten-year-old who was, from Lucy’s perspective, among the “big girls.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0000 }

Upon returning that evening, Robin remarked to Thirza, “School strikes me as wonderful entertainment. It turned out you were right about the difficulty of remaining motionless . . . I've observed that your statements are usually truthful . . . yet shifting your legs beneath the furniture provides considerable relief. Having numerous male companions for games is marvelous. My desk partner is Milty Gammon, who is great. Although he surpasses my height, my breadth exceeds his. The rear seating is preferable, yet occupying those spots requires limbs extended sufficiently to reach the ground. On his slate, Milty rendered a likeness of Nell that looked hideous, prompting my warning that repeating such depictions of Nell would result in my thrashing him during break time. My initial inclination was creating his portrait complete with tail and horns, but concern over damaging his sentiments held me back, since Nell teaches that causing emotional distress is strictly forbidden. Suffering hurt feelings is apparently a terrible ordeal. Should action be required, felling a boy physically is preferable to injuring his feelings. While claiming no fear of me, Milty offered to assign another identity to accommodate me, whereupon he erased the name of Nell and substituted Barbara Shaw's in print beneath the image. His dislike for Barbara stems from her addressing him as a sweet little boy and having once stroked his hair.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0001 }

Lucy stated demurely that she enjoyed school; nevertheless, she remained exceedingly silent, even by her own standards; and as dusk fell, upon Thirza instructing her to retire to bed on the upper floor, she paused and started weeping.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0002 }

“I’m . . . I’m scared,” she wept. “I . . . I don’t wish to ascend to the upper floor by myself in the pitch-black.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0003 }

“What idea have you put in your mind now?” Thirza asked. “I know you have retired to bed by yourself throughout the summer and have not been scared until now.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0004 }

Nell gathered Lucy up into her arms, gave her a compassionate cuddle, and murmured while she kept weeping,
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0005 }

“Disclose everything to Nell, my love. What is causing you fear?”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0006 }

“Of . . . of Mirabel Cotton’s uncle,” Lucy wept. “In school today, Mirabel Cotton related everything concerning her family to me. Almost all the people in her family are dead . . . every one of her grandfathers and grandmothers, along with a great many uncles and aunts. According to Mirabel, dying is a habit they have. Mirabel feels terribly proud about possessing such a large number of deceased relatives, and she described to me the cause of death for each one, as well as their final words and their appearance inside their coffins. Furthermore, Mirabel states that after his burial, a certain uncle of hers was spotted roaming about the house. Her mother observed him. The others do not bother me quite as much, but I am unable to stop reflecting on that uncle.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0007 }

Nell accompanied Lucy to the upper floor and remained beside her until sleep overtook her. On the following day, Mirabel Cotton was detained during the break and was made to comprehend, “gently but firmly,” that if one happened to be so unlucky as to have an uncle who insisted on wandering through dwellings following a proper burial, discussing that peculiar gentleman with a young classmate sharing one's desk lacked good taste. Mirabel considered this exceedingly severe. The Cottons possessed very little to brag about. In what manner could she maintain her standing with her fellow pupils if she was not allowed to profit from the ghost in her family?
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0008 }

The passing of September led into the gracious gold and crimson of October. Isolde visited one Friday evening.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0009 }

“I received a letter from Ella Kimball today, Nell, in which she invites us over to tea tomorrow afternoon so we can meet Irene Trent, her cousin from town. However, we are unable to take any of our horses, since they will every one be busy tomorrow, and your pony is lame . . . therefore I guess we will be unable to go.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0010 }

“Why can’t we walk?” proposed Nell. “If we return directly through the woods, we will hit the West Welby road close to the Kimball place. I traveled that route last winter, so I am familiar with the road. The distance is at most four miles, and walking all the way home won't be necessary because Oliver Kimball is certain to give us a ride. Having a reason will make him exceedingly happy, as he visits Carrie Mott and people claim that his father rarely permits him to take a horse.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0011 }

It was therefore agreed that they would go on foot, and they departed the next afternoon, travelling along Linger Lane toward the rear of the Abernethy farm, where they discovered a path entering the center of expanse upon expanse of shining beech and maple forests, which were completely transformed into a marvelous radiance of fire and gold, resting in a vast violet tranquility and calm.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0012 }

“Is it not as though the year is bowing in prayer inside a huge cathedral packed with soft, tinted light?” Nell asked wistfully. “Passing through it hastily feels wrong, doesn't it? Sprinting inside a church would be just as disrespectful.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0013 }

“Although we have to move quickly,” Isolde remarked, checking the time on her wrist. “Given how little time remains for us now.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0014 }

“Well, I’ll step out quickly, but do not request that I speak,” Nell said, moving faster. “My sole desire is to absorb the beauty of the day . . . It seems to me as though it is being offered to my lips like a goblet of light wine, and each step I take will be a sip.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0015 }

It might have been due to her being so preoccupied with “drinking it in” that Nell chose the left fork upon reaching a split in the path. Although the right path was the one she ought to have chosen, she subsequently regarded it as the luckiest error she ever made. Eventually, they emerged onto an isolated, grass-covered track, where the only visible objects were rows of young spruce trees.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0016 }

“Where on earth have we ended up?” asked Isolde, thoroughly confused. “We aren't on the road to West Welby.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0017 }

“No, Middle Welby’s base line road is what this is,” Nell stated, feeling quite embarrassed. “At the fork, I surely went the incorrect way. Although our exact location escapes me, Kimballs’ remains a full three miles away at least.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0018 }

“Because it is already four thirty,” Isolde remarked, glancing hopeless at her timepiece, “we will not be able to arrive before five. Our arrival will happen once they finish their tea, which means they will face the full nuisance of preparing ours a second time.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0019 }

“It would be best for us to head back home,” meekly offered Nell. Isolde, however, thought about it and then rejected the idea.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0020 }

“No, we might just as well proceed to pass the evening, seeing that we have traveled all this way.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0021 }

Advancing another couple of yards, the girls arrived at a spot where the road split once more.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0022 }

“Which one of these are we taking?” Isolde asked, sounding uncertain.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0023 }

Nell gave a shake of her head.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0024 }

“I am uncertain, and making further errors is beyond our means. This gate and path head straight into the forest. On the far end, there has to be a home. Let’s head down and ask.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0025 }

“What a romantic old lane this it,” Isolde remarked, while they traversed its winding path. It stretched beneath ancient, majestic fir trees with overhead intertwining limbs, producing an endless darkness where moss alone was able to thrive. Earthy forest beds bordered both sides, traversed now and then by descending shafts of light. Everything felt extraordinarily quiet and distant, as though the earth and its anxieties were miles removed.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0026 }

“It seems to me that we are strolling in a magical wood,” Nell uttered softly. “Isolde, do you think we will ever manage to return to the actual world? In a moment, I believe we will arrive at a castle containing a bewitched princess.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0027 }

Rounding the subsequent bend, there appeared in their view not a grand palace, but a tiny dwelling nearly as astonishing as a palace would have proved in this region of traditional wooden farmhouses, every one so similar in overall traits that they might have sprouted from identical seed. Nell paused abruptly in delight, and Isolde cried out, “Oh, I know where we are now. That is the little stone house where Miss Rosalind Penrose lives . . . Echo Cottage, she calls it, I think. I’ve often heard of it but I’ve never seen it before. Isn’t it a romantic spot?”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0028 }

“It is the most charming and lovely spot I have ever witnessed or conceived,” Nell expressed with joy. “It appears just like an excerpt from a fairy tale or a vision.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0029 }

Constructed from rough, unpolished blocks of red Island sandstone, the building featured low eaves, a small pointed roof pierced by a pair of dormer windows with unusual wooden hoods above them, and two massive chimneys. Richly draped across the entire structure, ivy clung effortlessly to the coarse masonry, its leaves transformed by autumn frosts into stunning shades of bronze and deep wine-red.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0030 }

An oblong garden, into which opened the lane gate where the girls were standing, was situated before the house. It was bounded on one side by the house; an old stone dyke enclosed it on the three others, being so overgrown with moss and grass and ferns that a high, green bank was what it resembled. Over it, the tall, dark spruces spread their palm-like branches on the right and left; a little meadow, green with clover aftermath, was below it, however, sloping down to the blue loop of the Welby River. In sight was no other house or clearing . . . covered with feathery young firs were nothing but hills and valleys.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0031 }

“I wonder what kind of individual Miss Penrose might be,” pondered Isolde while they unlatched the garden gate. “It is said that her ways are quite strange.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0032 }

“In that case, she will prove interesting,” Nell declared firmly. “Odd individuals invariably manage to be that much, regardless of what other qualities they possess or lack. Didn’t I say to you that our journey would lead to a spellbound castle? I was certain those elves had not spun enchantment across that path without reason.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0033 }

“However, Miss Rosalind Penrose can scarcely be considered an enchanted princess,” Isolde chuckled. “She is a spinster . . . I have been told that she is forty-five and her hair is completely gray.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0034 }

“Oh, that is merely a fraction of the enchantment,” Nell declared with certainty. “Deep down she remains youthful and lovely . . . and she would emerge glowing and beautiful once more if we just understood the way to break the magic. Yet we lack that knowledge . . . that secret belongs solely and perpetually to the prince . . . and the prince meant for Miss Rosalind has not arrived so far. Maybe he has met with a disastrous misfortune . . . even if such an outcome violates the rules of every fairy tale.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0035 }

“I fear his arrival occurred a while back and his departure followed,” stated Isolde. “It is reported that her engagement to Stephen Stanhope . . . the father of Cedric . . . existed during their youth. However, a disagreement arose, causing them to separate.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0036 }

“Be quiet,” Nell cautioned. “That door is unclosed.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0037 }

In the porch beneath the ivy tendrils, the girls stopped and knocked upon the open door. A patter of footsteps sounded from within, and a somewhat strange small figure appeared . . . a girl near fourteen years old, possessing a face covered in freckles, a nose that was snubbed, a mouth of such width that it appeared to literally reach “from ear to ear,” and a pair of long fair hair braids fastened with a pair of huge blue ribbon bows.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0038 }

“Is Miss Penrose in?” Isolde inquired.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0039 }

“Indeed, ma’am. Step inside, ma’am. I shall inform Miss Rosalind of your arrival, ma’am. Her ladyship is on the upper floor, ma’am.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0040 }

With those words the diminutive handmaiden darted away, and the girls, remaining by themselves, surveyed their surroundings with joyous eyes. Inside, this marvelous small house proved every bit as captivating as it appeared from the outside.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0041 }

Low-ceilinged, the room possessed a pair of square windows with small panes, which muslin-frilled curtains draped. Aged as all the furniture was, its maintenance was so fine and neat that it produced a delightful impression. However, one must honestly concede that the item possessing the greatest appeal to a couple of robust girls after walking four miles in the autumn breeze was a table, which held a spread of delicacies on light blue china, whereas small golden ferns strewn across the tablecloth imparted to it what Nell would have called “a festal air.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0042 }

“Company for tea must be expected by Miss Rosalind,” she murmured. “Six places have been laid. However, what a strange little child she possesses. A messenger from pixy land is what she resembled. The way could likely have been given to us by her, I assume, yet seeing Miss Rosalind was my desire. S . . . s . . . sh, coming is she.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0043 }

And with that Miss Rosalind Penrose appeared in the doorway. The girls were taken so unawares that good manners were forgotten, and they just stared. Without realizing it, they had been anticipating the conventional sort of aged spinster from their past experience . . . an inclined-to-be bony individual, possessing neat gray hair and glasses. Something less resembling Miss Rosalind could not conceivably be pictured.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0044 }

She was a tiny woman possessing snow-white hair that was lovely, wavy, and thick, thoughtfully set in flattering puffs and coils. An almost youthful face appeared below it, having rosy cheeks, sweet lips, large gentle brown eyes, and dimples . . . truly dimples. Her dress was a particularly delicate cream muslin adorned with light-colored roses . . . an attire that would have appeared absurdly young on the majority of women her age, yet it fitted Miss Rosalind so flawlessly that it never crossed your mind.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0045 }

“Belinda the Fourth mentioned that you wanted to speak with me,” she stated, employing a voice that suited her look.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0046 }

“We intended to inquire about the correct route to West Welby,” Isolde said. “Mr. Kimball invited us to tea, however, taking the incorrect track while traveling through the woods brought us out to the base line rather than the West Welby road. Should we turn right or left when we reach your gate?”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0047 }

“On the left,” stated Miss Rosalind, casting a doubtful look toward the table where her tea was set. Subsequently, she gave a cry, as though propelled by a brief, unexpected wave of determination,
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0048 }

“However, oh, will you not remain and partake of tea with me? I beg of you, do. The tea at Mr. Kimball’s will be finished prior to your arrival there. Furthermore, Belinda the Fourth and I shall be exceedingly happy to host you.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0049 }

Isolde offered Nell a silent, questioning glance.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0050 }

“We’d like to stay,” Nell stated without delay, having resolved that she wished to learn further details about this astonishing Miss Rosalind, “provided it doesn't put you out. However, you are anticipating additional visitors, aren’t you?”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0051 }

Miss Rosalind cast another glance toward her tea table, her cheeks turning red.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0052 }

“I am aware you will consider me terribly silly,” she stated. “I am silly . . . and I feel humiliated about it whenever I am caught, but only when I am caught. I am not awaiting anyone . . . I was merely imagining that I was. You understand, I felt very isolated. I adore society . . . meaning, the proper sort of society . . . but hardly any individuals ever visit this place since it is extremely remote. Belinda the Fourth felt isolated as well. Consequently, I simply imagined I was about to host a tea party. I prepared food for it . . . and adorned the table for it . . . and arranged it using my mother’s wedding china . . . and I put on fine clothes for it.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0053 }

In Isolde’s private opinion, Miss Rosalind was just as odd as rumor had described her to be. Imagine a forty-five-year-old woman pretending to host a tea party, exactly like a young girl would! Nell, however, with her glowing eyes, cried out in delight,
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0054 }

“Ah, is imagining things something you do as well?”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0055 }

Hearing “too” made Miss Rosalind recognize someone who shared her own feelings.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0056 }

“Yes, I do,” she admitted with courage. “Naturally it is foolish for a person of my age. However, why be an unattached elderly woman if one cannot act foolishly whenever desired, provided no one is harmed? One requires certain rewards. Occasionally, I doubt I could survive without imagining things. Usually I am not discovered doing it, and Belinda the Fourth remains silent. Nonetheless, I am pleased to be discovered this afternoon, because you are actually here and I have prepared tea for you. Would you like to ascend to the guest bedroom to remove your hats? You will find it behind the white door at the top of the staircase. I have to hurry into the kitchen to ensure Belinda the Fourth does not allow the tea to boil. Although Belinda the Fourth is an excellent girl, she tends to let the tea boil.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0057 }

Miss Rosalind hurried away toward the kitchen, her mind set on hospitality, while the girls made their path upstairs to the spare room, a space every bit as white as its own door, illuminated through the ivy-draped dormer window and appearing, as Nell said, “like the place where happy dreams grew.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0058 }

“This is a real adventure, don’t you think?” Isolde asked. “And isn’t Miss Rosalind delightful, even though she is slightly peculiar? She does not look at all like an old maid.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0059 }

“In my opinion, her appearance resembles the way music sounds,” Nell replied.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0060 }

As they descended, Miss Rosalind entered with the teapot, followed by Belinda the Fourth, who appeared thoroughly delighted as she held a dish of warm biscuits.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0061 }

“At present, I need you to give me your names,” Miss Rosalind said. “It makes me very happy that you are young girls. Young girls are dear to me. Pretending to be a girl myself comes so naturally when I am in their company. I really despise” . . . making a slight face . . . “accepting that I am advanced in years. Now, which one is which . . . simply for the sake of convenience? Isolde Pembroke? And Nell Harcourt? Is it all right if I act as though our acquaintance goes back a century and address you as Nell and Isolde from this moment on?”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0062 }

“You, may” both the girls said at the same time.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0063 }

“Then let us merely sit down comfortably and consume all of it,” Miss Rosalind remarked with joy. “Belinda, take your seat at the bottom and assist with the chicken. Having prepared the sponge cake and doughnuts is such a stroke of luck. Naturally, making them for non-existent visitors was silly . . . I am aware Belinda the Fourth held that opinion, wasn't that your thought, Belinda? Yet you observe how favorably the situation developed. Naturally they would not have gone to waste, since Belinda the Fourth and I were capable of consuming them as time passed. However, sponge cake does not become better over time.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0064 }

It was a joyful and unforgettable feast; and upon its conclusion, everyone walked out into the garden, which rested in the enchantment of dusk.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0065 }

“I really believe you possess the most beautiful spot right here,” Isolde remarked, gazing about herself with admiration.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0066 }

“For what reason is it named Echo Cottage?” inquired Nell.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0067 }

“Belinda,” Miss Rosalind said, “walk inside the house and fetch the small tin horn hanging above the shelf with the clock.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0068 }

Belinda the Fourth bounded away and came back bringing the horn.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0069 }

“Puff on it, Belinda,” Miss Rosalind ordered.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0070 }

Belinda therefore sounded the horn, producing a somewhat harsh and grating note. A brief quiet followed . . . before a host of enchanted echoes rang out from the forest across the water, soft, fleeting, and clear, resembling the collective sounding of every "horn of elfland" in the fading light. Nell and Isolde cried out with pleasure.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0071 }

“Laugh at present, Belinda . . . giggle with great volume.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0072 }

Belinda, who likely would have complied had Miss Rosalind instructed her to stand on her head, got up onto the stone bench and chuckled in a loud, hearty manner. The echoes returned, appearing like a crowd of pixy folk mimicking her chuckling within the purple woods and beside the fir-bordered points.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0073 }

“Individuals continuously hold my echoes in great esteem,” declared Miss Rosalind, as though she owned those echoes herself. “I adore them personally. They serve as excellent companions . . . provided one uses a bit of imagination. When the evenings are peaceful, Belinda the Fourth and I frequently remain outside here to entertain ourselves using them. Belinda, retrieve the horn and hang it attentively where it belongs.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0074 }

“Why is she named Belinda the Fourth by you?” inquired Isolde, whose curiosity regarding this matter was about to overflow.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0075 }

“Simply so I do not confuse her with the different Charlottas in my mind,” Miss Rosalind remarked solemnly. “Because they appear so similar, distinguishing them is impossible. Actually, her name is not Belinda whatsoever. It is . . . let me think . . . what could it be? My belief is that it is Leonora . . . indeed, Leonora is correct. You see, the situation is like this. A decade ago, when my mother passed away, remaining here by myself was impossible . . . and covering the pay for an adult girl was beyond my means. Therefore, I arranged for young Belinda Bowman to live with me in exchange for room, board, and garments. Belinda was genuinely her name . . . she represented Belinda the First. Thirteen was her exact age. She remained in my home until reaching sixteen, at which point she departed for Boston, as superior opportunities awaited her there. At that time, her sister arrived to reside with me. Julietta was her name . . . it seems to me Mrs. Bowman possessed a fondness for extravagant names . .. yet her appearance mirrored Belinda’s to such an extent that I continually addressed her by that name . . . and it caused her no distress. Consequently, I simply ceased attempting to recall her actual name. She became Belinda the Second, and following her departure, Evelina arrived as Belinda the Third. Currently, Belinda the Fourth is with me; however, upon turning sixteen . . . her current age being fourteen . . . she will likewise desire to leave for Boston, and what my course of action will be at that point is truly unknown to me. Among the Bowman daughters, Belinda the Fourth is the final one, as well as the finest. The alternate Charlottas consistently made it clear they considered my imaginative pretending foolish, whereas Belinda the Fourth refrains from doing so, regardless of her actual opinions. Whatever opinions people hold regarding me causes me no concern, provided they refrain from making it apparent to me.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0076 }

“Well,” Isolde stated while gazing mournfully at the sinking sun. “I guess we ought to depart if getting to Mr. Kimball’s prior to nightfall is our goal. Our time here was delightful, Miss Penrose.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0077 }

“Will you not visit me once more?” Miss Rosalind begged.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0078 }

Tall Nell wrapped her arm around the small lady.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0079 }

“Truly we will,” she pledged. “Because we have found you, our visits will become overly frequent. Yes, it is time for us to depart . . . ‘we must wrench ourselves away,’ to quote Cedric Stanhope each time he visits Grey Shutters.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0080 }

“Cedric Stanhope?” Miss Rosalind’s tone shifted slightly. “What is his identity? I was under the impression that no person with that name resided in Brierley.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0081 }

Annoyance at her own carelessness washed over Nell. At the moment Cedric’s name escaped her lips, she had failed to remember the past love affair of Miss Rosalind.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0082 }

“He is a young student whom I teach,” she clarified in a unhurried manner. “He arrived from Boston during the previous year so that he could reside beside his grandmother, Mrs. Stanhope, who lives on the shore road.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0083 }

“Does Stephen Stanhope claim him as a son?” inquired Miss Rosalind, leaning down toward the flowerbed that shared her name in order to conceal her countenance.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0084 }

“Yes.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0085 }

“Each of you girls will get a cluster of lavender from me,” Miss Rosalind remarked cheerfully, acting as though the reply to her query had gone unheard. “Don’t you find it remarkably sweet? It was always a favorite of Mother’s. Many years back, she established these borders. Because he cherished it so much, Father chose Rosalind for my name. His introduction to mother occurred when her brother brought him to see her family in East Welby. It was love at first sight for him; moreover, when they placed him in the guest room bed for the night, the lavender-perfumed sheets kept him awake through the dark hours thinking about her. From that point on, he adored lavender’s fragrance . . . which explains his choice for my name. Make sure you return before long, my dear girls. Belinda the Fourth and I will be eagerly awaiting your arrival.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0086 }

She unlatched the entryway beneath the fir trees so that they could go by. In an instant, she appeared aged and fatigued; the bright luminosity had vanished from her features; her final smile remained as delightfully youthful as it had always been, yet as the girls turned to look back from the initial bend of the path, they observed her resting upon the ancient stone seat beneath the silver poplar at the center of the garden, her head resting heavily upon her hand.
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0087 }

“It is true that she seems lonely,” Isolde remarked in a quiet voice. “We ought to visit her frequently.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0088 }

“My belief is that her mother and father assigned her the sole correct and appropriate name she could ever have received,” Nell remarked. “Had they lacked the vision to call her Elizabeth, Nellie, or Muriel, she would still have needed to be named Rosalind regardless, in my opinion. It brings to mind sweetness, ancient elegance, and ‘silk attire.’ On the other hand, my own name merely tastes of bread and butter, patchwork, and domestic tasks.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0089 }

“Oh, I disagree,” Isolde remarked. “To my mind, Nell appears truly dignified and regal. However, Kerrenhappuch would appeal to me if you occurred to be named that. It seems to me that individuals render their names pleasant or unpleasant solely through their own character. Names such as Flossie or Tibby are insufferable to me at present, though prior to meeting the Tulk girls, I considered them quite charming.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0090 }

“Isolde, that is a wonderful thought,” Nell remarked with great enthusiasm. “Existing in a way that adorns your name, even though it lacked beauty initially . . . causing it to represent a concept so charming and agreeable in human minds that they fail to consider it on its own. I appreciate it, Isolde.”
{: #nw-v02-c21-p0091 }
